children: An artificial-intelligence startup with only 14 employees has reached a
$10 billion valuation
, highlighting just how aggressively investors are still betting on agentic AI despite growing scrutiny around the sector's valuations.
Instinct said Monday it raised an additional
$1 billion
from Sequoia Capital, Benchmark Capital and Coatue.
The size of the valuation is striking because Instinct remains in early access and has built its business with a tiny workforce.
Founded by Noah Shinn, Instinct is developing a personal AI agent designed to complete everyday tasks rather than simply answer questions.

Users can text or call the agent to plan a road trip, order groceries or cancel forgotten subscriptions. The system can then use its own phone and computer interfaces to carry out those tasks from start to finish.
Instinct is also expanding beyond basic requests.
Its
Instinct Concierge
service is designed for higher-touch tasks such as making phone calls and booking services, while the company's
Trusted Person Network
allows different Instinct agents to communicate and coordinate plans on behalf of users.
The latest funding will be used to expand access to the product while the company continues developing its personal-agent technology.
The deal lands at a sensitive moment for AI investors.

Valuations across the industry have come under increasing scrutiny as investors question whether enormous spending on AI infrastructure and software will translate into similarly large near-term revenues.
Investor takeaway
Instinct's $10 billion valuation shows that investors remain willing to assign enormous value to companies that could become central interfaces for agentic AI.
But the company also represents the valuation debate in its most extreme form.

With just 14 employees and a product still in early access, future value depends heavily on adoption, retention and whether users ultimately trust AI agents to take real-world actions on their behalf.
The key metrics to watch are user growth, task completion rates, monetization and whether Instinct can turn convenience into a defensible platform.
If personal agents become a primary way consumers interact with services, the upside could be significant.
If adoption develops more slowly, the gap between Instinct's current valuation and its commercial scale could become much harder to justify.

title: 14-Person AI Startup Lands Stunning $10 Billion Valuation
